items.body: The online casino landscape has transformed entertainment, offering unparalleled reach to online gaming sites from the comfort of home. With thousands of options available worldwide, selecting a trustworthy and dependable platform requires thorough evaluation of licensing, security measures, payment options, and responsible gaming safeguards. Understanding License Requirements and Oversight in Internet Gaming Platforms Licensing acts as the foundation of legitimacy for any online casino operator, providing players with assurance that operations meet stringent regulatory standards. Reputable jurisdictions such as the UK Gambling Commission, Malta Gaming Authority, and Gibraltar Regulatory Authority maintain detailed regulations governing fair play, fiscal openness, and ethical gambling standards. These governing authorities perform detailed vetting processes on operators, mandate periodic reviews of gaming software, and establish dispute settlement procedures to protect player interests throughout their gaming experience. When assessing a casino’s credentials, confirm that licensing information is displayed clearly on the website, typically in the footer area with clickable logos linking to the regulator’s official verification page. Reputable casinos display their license numbers openly and offer clear details about their business registration details and ownership structure. Be wary of platforms claiming regulation from obscure jurisdictions with minimal oversight, as these often miss the regulatory mechanisms necessary to protect players from unfair practices or financial disputes that may occur during play. The regulatory framework also determines which markets an operator can lawfully operate in, with licensed casinos restricted to accepting players from approved territories where they hold valid permissions. UK-licensed platforms, for instance, must adhere to strict advertising standards, implement compulsory self-exclusion programmes, and contribute to gambling addiction studies and treatment programmes. Understanding these regulatory distinctions helps players recognize platforms committed to ethical business practices, ensuring that their selected operator operates under meaningful supervision rather than merely displaying visually impressive yet ultimately hollow certification badges on their homepage. Important Security Features to Consider Security should be your primary concern when selecting a gaming platform, as you’ll be sharing confidential financial and personal information. Trusted platforms invest heavily in cutting-edge security systems to protect player data from online attacks and unauthorized access. Learning about the key security features helps you recognize sites that take player protection seriously and uphold industry-standard safeguards. The best established casino websites display their security credentials prominently on their websites, making it simple for users to confirm their dedication to safety. These features work together to create several protective layers, ensuring your gaming experience remains secure from registration through withdrawal. Getting to know these critical safety features allows you to make informed decisions about where to play. Secure Socket Layer Encryption and Information Security Secure Socket Layer (SSL) encryption is the foundation of online security, creating an encrypted connection between your device and the gaming platform’s servers. You can confirm SSL protection by checking for the padlock icon in your browser’s address bar and verifying the URL begins with “https” rather than “http”. This technology scrambles your data during transmission, rendering it unreadable to anyone attempting to intercept it. Leading gaming platforms use 128-bit or 256-bit SSL encryption, the equivalent standard utilized by banks and financial institutions worldwide. This level of protection ensures that your login details, payment details, and personal data remain secure throughout all transactions. Sites without proper SSL encryption must be avoided, as they expose your financial data exposed to hackers and identity thieves. Secure Payment Methods and Payment Alternatives Trustworthy gaming sites offer a diverse range of safe payment options, including established options like Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Skrill, and Neteller. The presence of trusted payment companies indicates that the platform has met strict security requirements and undergone comprehensive review procedures. These payment companies only partner with legitimate operators who maintain high security requirements. Look for platforms that support contemporary payment methods such as e-wallets, prepaid cards, and cryptocurrency options which provide extra levels of anonymity and security. Transparent fee structures, fair withdrawal caps, and clearly stated processing times are signs of a trustworthy platform. Steer clear of sites that only accept obscure payment methods or digital currencies only, as this may indicate potential issues with legitimacy or regulatory compliance. Account Identity Confirmation Legitimate gaming platforms implement Know Your Customer (KYC) requirements that require players to authenticate themselves prior to initiating withdrawals. This procedure typically involves submitting government-issued identification, residential documentation, and sometimes payment method verification. While this may seem inconvenient, it’s actually a positive sign that the operator takes regulatory compliance and fraud detection with priority. The verification process shields both you and the gaming platform from illegal activity, financial crimes, and minors accessing games. Legitimate operators clearly explain their identity requirements upfront and complete verification promptly, generally within 24-48 hours. Be wary of sites which either have zero verification requirements or request excessive documentation exceeding normal procedures, as both situations may indicate problematic operations. Assessing Game Fairness and Gaming Software Developers The reliability of casino platforms confirms whether outcomes are truly unpredictable or altered in the casino’s benefit. Reputable platforms work alongside established software developers like Microgaming, NetEnt, Playtech, and Evolution Gaming, whose offerings go through comprehensive third-party audits. These companies use licensed RNG technology (RNGs) that confirm each spin or card deal remains completely unpredictable and equitable for all players. Third-party verification organizations such as eCOGRA, iTech Labs, and Gaming Laboratories International (GLI) verify that gaming software meets rigorous fairness standards. Check for certification seals prominently displayed on the casino’s website, typically in the footer area. These organisations perform regular audits and release payout percentage reports, giving players transparent insight into the mathematical fairness of games available on the platform. Return-to-Player (RTP) percentages show the theoretical amount a game returns to players over longer gaming sessions. Trustworthy platforms showcase RTP information transparently for each game, with percentages generally falling from 94% to 98% for slots and greater for table games. Steer clear of sites that hide this information or offer games with suspiciously low RTP rates, as clear disclosure of game performance demonstrates the operator’s dedication to fairness and user experience. Provably fair technology constitutes the forefront of transparency in gaming, particularly in cryptocurrency-based platforms. This cryptographic method enables players to confirm the integrity of each gaming round on their own, removing the need to trust the casino’s assurances alone. While not currently standard on all platforms, the availability of provably fair games or detailed fairness documentation shows a casino’s dedication to maintaining the top standards of game fairness and customer confidence. Checking out Player Feedback and Assessing Reputation Before depositing your money to any platform, performing detailed investigations through user feedback and reputation checks provides invaluable insights into operational standards and reliability. User Reviews and Community Forums Real user testimonials on third-party platforms reveal actual accounts with withdrawal processing times, support team efficiency, and overall satisfaction levels that promotional content rarely disclose. Engaged gaming communities on platforms like Reddit, Casinomeister, and AskGamblers provide transparent discussions where players exchange both favorable outcomes and cautionary tales about online casinos they’ve experienced. Casino Review Review Sites Industry analysis websites utilize expert reviewers who carefully assess gaming sites based on license verification, fairness protocols, dependable payment systems, and customer support quality standards. Credible review sites use open methodologies, disclose affiliate relationships, and frequently refresh their assessments to reflect current operational performance rather than outdated information. Safer Gambling Tools and Player Assistance A trustworthy casino platform prioritises player wellbeing by offering comprehensive responsible gambling tools. These should include deposit limits, session timers, reality checks, and self-exclusion options that allow you to maintain control over your gaming habits. Look for platforms that partner with organisations like GamCare, BeGambleAware, or Gamblers Anonymous, providing easy access to professional support services. Quality customer support serves as your lifeline when issues arise, making it essential to test responsiveness before committing financially. Reputable platforms offer multiple contact channels including live chat, email, and telephone support, with representatives available around the clock. Before depositing funds, send a test enquiry to evaluate response times and the helpfulness of staff answers. Comprehensive FAQ sections and detailed help centres also indicate a professional operation that values transparent communication with its player base. The casino’s approach to responsible gaming protection shows its genuine nature and operational standards. Check whether the site shows responsible gambling messages prominently, requires age verification during registration, and educates support staff to recognise problematic gaming habits. Trustworthy operators will not push you to keep gambling once you’ve set boundaries and should provide account closure options easy without unnecessary delays. These safeguarding practices, paired with honest terms, form the foundation for a protected and fun playing atmosphere that values your wellbeing over earnings.

items.body: “Monte” is a louder, brighter turn for Helena Recalde. The Ecuadorian bassist, singer and composer, long settled in France, usually works Andean melody and Afro-Pacific rhythm into jazz, and here she keeps the Afro-Pacific rhythm but pushes it louder and brighter, electric guitars and a balafon over layered percussion, her bass holding the centre. The refrain is a summons, “El monte me llama”, the mountain calling her by name. In the verses that call comes from a jungle in trouble: it stirs, it wears thin, it hurts, but no one is listening. Recalde recorded “Monte” with Nicolas Gaud on guitar, Vanesa García on drums, Muriel Gastebois on balafon, Sebastián on percussion and Aurora Alquinta Monsalve on backing vocals, under the direction of French saxophonist Julien Lourau. items.body: Review by Matti — What a strange (and failing) attempt to demonstrate "a wide range of music" known as progressive rock. I have, out of sheer curiosity and a wish to expand my knowledge on lesser bands, borrowed and listened to numerous prog compilations, and this 2-CD set must be the most oriented towards heavy (and frankly, not always so progressive) stuff of the late sixties/early seventies, favouring edgy electronic guitars and Hammond organ. The person who compiled this obviously likes hard rock, blues rock and jazz-rock tinged with psychedelia, and doesn't care at all about the more delicate, classical music influenced prog. The band choices are guaranteed to raise eyebrows of prog enthusiasts, both for the included acts and for the absence of myriads of standout prog bands. The four-page liner notes are at times just ridiculous. (All words in my review marked with "s are quotations.) The actual information on the tracks is rather inadequate. For example no source albums are marked, only occasionally mentioned in those vaguely chatty liner notes.There's Status Quo and TWO of the 60's line-ups preceding it! I don't hear much of prog, and yet "You'll witness a world-class progression, if a definition of the prog-word is what you're looking for". Uriah Heep is represented by two tracks (both good and quite well known). Eventually you'll get bands like Atomic Rooster, Colosseum, Tempest, Blonde On Blonde and Quatermass. Often the bands with an eclectic oeuvre are represented by a relatively hard rocking piece. Man (1969), for example. There is a bunch of essential prog bands, and especially on them the liner notes and the offered information are very haphazard. Is there really an ELP song titled 'Brain Salad Surgery'? Is Fruupp's 'Old Tyme Future' on one of their albums, for I don't remember such song? The liner notes ask "who wrote epic prog anthems better than Procol Harum" ('Conquistador', The live version with an orchestra), which is funny in a sense that the epic side of prog is pretty absent altogether. I'm baffled by the VdGG choice 'Bunsho' (Live at Metropolis) since I don't recall the source album, and also the composing credits (Andrew/ Banton/ Randolp) sound odd to me. I appreciate the inclusions of Caravan (1970), Spirogyra, Titus Groan, Colosseum II (1976) and Comus (1971, and yet a track NOT from their cassic album, right?). I would categorize Fire (1970) more into psychedelia than prog, despite being "delivered by master musicians, later of the Strawbs stable". The whole is very much British oriented, with a few exceptions: Amon Duul II (1969) of the main time line, and, representing the newer times, Voivod from Canada and Tides From Nebula from Poland. Gee, what a way to expand the timeline, by including "an experimental thrash metal act" (the liner notes don't even mention they are covering the Syd Barrett era Pink Floyd) and "a wonderfully far-out slab of post-rock noise", and Zoroaster's "quasi-psychedelic take on doom metal".The eighties are represented in an equally peculiar way. A quotation: "throughout the 1980s and 90s, The prog flag was flown by a New (or at least, not old) group of acts. Among them were the mighty John Lee's Barclay James Harvest, represented here by the John Lees-fronted variant of the two touring version of BJH" - whaaat?? The other 80's pick is the early instrumental era of Twelfth Night, which is delightful as a very rarely heard thing, but Again one would wish to have informative liner notes instead of a vague mentioning of "neo prog (as the new music was inevitably dubbed)".So, I believe I managed to showcase the rather unorthodox and uneducated take on "progressive rock". If the liner notes would have openly admitted the favouring of certain music styles and excused the omittance of the more classic (symphonic) prog, that would be easier to accept. Did I get any happy discoveries? Yes, one. I had never heard of Woody Kern, but their flute-starring jazz-rock sounds great.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — British Jazz-Rockers whose career lasted four years during which they were able to produce three very solid Jazz-Rock Fusion albums, starting with this one. The band's debut album was released in the UK by Island Records in October of 1970, in the US by the Capitol label.1. "I'm Reaching Out on All Sides" (5:14) a simple straight Blues song that the band tries to jazz up with its horns in the fashion of bands like Blood, Sweat & Tears and Chicago though one can definitely hear the influence of any band the Steve Winwood has participated in by this time (The Spencer Davis Group, Traffic, Blind Faith). The music slowly increases in intensity over the opening three minutes, even as singer J.W. Hodgkinson sings in an Alex Ligertwood-type or Roger Wootton-like sound and style, building up a and somewhat unsettling or 'scary' hypnotic effect, but then, in the fourth minute, the two saxes appear with emphatic punctuation accents in the style and tradition of the famous MEMPHIS HORNS to take us into an even-more psychedelic WHO-like motif (complete with a PETE TOWNSEND-like singing voice). The effect of this two-person horn section is powerful enough to make me re-listen to the song over and over to uncover how, in fact, the band is achieving such an impressive "full horn" effect. (9/10)2. "What Did I Say About the Box, Jack?" (8:20) despite a dynamic and powerful flute-and-sax-led Jazz-Rock opening and an ensuing "I'm a Man"-like organ chord progression over which composer Dick Morrissey performs quite a wild and enthusiastic flute solo, the main body of this song is built over organist John Mealing's four chord minor blues progression--a progression that was obviously borrowed from fellow Brit guitarist Peter Green's Latin-Blues songs "I Loved Another Woman" (from Fleetwood Mac's self-titled debut album) and "Black Magic Woman" (which was somewhat borrowed from John Mayall & The Blues Breakers' version of Otis Redding's "All Your Love" two years previously), the latter of which first appeared as a single, released by Fleetwood Mac in March of 1968--long before it became a household name via SANTANA's Abraxis album (both released in the Autumn of 1970). The Latinized minor blues chord progression then becomes the support bed for guitarist Terry Smith's extended lead, the two-sax "horn section"'s accents, and, later, some smooth sax soloing to take us well into the seventh and eighth minutes. I have to say that I am impressed with the way these guys can cobble together a song! (18.125/20)3. "What Can a Friend Say?" (6:28) switching to a slightly-muted guitar tone, Terry Smith gives us an excellent STEPHEN STILLS impression on his lead guitar as the band establishes a very full, very dynamic Jazz-Rock motif for a vocal performance that reminds me of MURRAY HEAD in the iconic role of Judas in Andrew Lloyd-Weber's Jesus Christ Superstar. A very aggressive tenor sax solo takes over the lead in the middle of the song, presenting a very strong, very spirited performance as the equally-inspired rhythm section pushes and propells the music along in quite the BLOOD, SWEAT & TEARS fashion. Again, a powerfully-designed and amplified Jazzed-up Rock song. (9.125/10)4. "Woman, Can You See (What This Big Thing Is All About)?" (4:01) Side Two begins with another blues-based chord progression and melody line that is elevated by speed and power of the musicians' dynamic energy. Solid and powerful. (9/10)5. "Raise the Level of Your Conscious Mind" (3:11) using the Jazz-Rock medium to elevate the spiritual wisdom of the Hippie Age! It's as if the L.A. positivity is being taken over by the San Francisco blues-rock scene. I like the message: I can see it being effective as a medium for gaining audience participation (which was, apparently, one of the band's strenghts). (8.75/10)6. "Dockland" (5:21) here again I find the band trying to tap into the social-political consciousness that musicians all over America were trying to squeeze into: CROSBY, STILLS, NASH & YOUNG and THE ASSOCIATION. It's good but now feeling rather dated. The final minute shows the band picking up from one of their previous songs--where the vocalist seems to want to sing about important things in a form most familiar to the radio world via the music coming from West End/Broadway-like stage musicals. (8.875/10)7. "The Promised Land" (4:31) the hippie spirit of consciousness raising is again felt rather strongly in both the lyrics and the uplifting theatric/Christian music Singer J.W. Hodgkinson certainly comes across as feeling genuine in his backing of the lyrics he's singing. Heck! The whole band continues to come exploding through any haze or lethargy with their amazingly intrepid performances! (And, yes, I love the Stephen Stills guitar tone Terry has decided to settle into over the course of the second half of the album--since "What Can a Friend Say?".) (8.75/10)Total Time 37:06The band was obviously made up of experienced, well-trained musicians, at the same time it is equally obvious that they are rising out of the UK's well-steeped Blues/Blues-Rock scene. What I find most remarkable about the music on this album is the songwriters' abilities to cobble together riffs, themes, and styles borrowed from or inspired by other songs, bands, and musicians while rendering them interesting, layered, and each song multi-varied/multi-movement. It's still a mystery to me how this band & production crew got the powerful horn section sound out of two saxophone players! B+/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of Jazz-Rock that I'm almost ready and willing to bump up to masterpiece status based upon the consistently upbeat power and force of its music and mature whole-band performances.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — With the release of his third album, James LaBrie and his solo band established themselves as arecognizable entity in the world of progressive metal. 'Impermanent Resonance' was released in 2013on Inside Out Music, expanding upon the stylistic searching of its predecessor - 2010's 'StaticImpulse'. LaBrie is once again joined by guitarist Marco Sfogli (who would go on to join PFM),drummer Peter Wildoer, bass player Ray Riendeau, and keyboardist Matt Guillory, practicallypreserving the lineup that had worked on the aforementioned previous album. And truth be told, thereis very little separating these two releases, stylistically and production-wise. The listener ispresented with a very modern, upbeat, (and sometimes overproduced) modern metal that bridges theprogressive and alternative genres in a pretty successful, commercially inclined way.'Impermanent Resonance', much like its predecessor, but perhaps more ostensibly, explores a melodicdeath metal/metalcore aesthetic, with drummer Peter Wildore singing all the harsh vocals heard onthis album. The entire record is pretty song-oriented, and the extended use of electronics and fast-paced synth leads reminds me of bands like Motionless in White and The Devil Wears Prada, who alsolike to use lots of synths. This solo project from James LaBrie definitely separates itself from theDream Theater sonic trajectory, but the inevitable comparison between the two bands allows us tounderstand that the melodic and highly digestible prog metal of 'Impermanent Resonance' is lessappealing than the sophisticated prog theatrics of LaBrie's main band. Nevertheless, this is a goodeffort, on which I have found the songs 'Agony', 'Back on the Ground', 'Lost in the Fire', 'Destinedto Burn' and 'I Will Not Break' to be really enjoyable.

items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comA wonderful album, overflowing with power! I am one of those people who actually trusts the recommendations suggested by streaming platform algorithms, because more often than not they lead me to real gems. That was precisely the case with Maruja. Their name caught my attention, but their music completely blew my mind. What this band from England delivers across eight tracks and fifty minutes is a carousel of sounds that move from experimental jazz to hip hop, passing through alternative and progressive rock, all wrapped in a defiant punk spirit. The result is a powerful blend of explosive passages and groovy moments that create an exquisite balance, although your mind will probably linger on the most intense, noisy, high-energy sections. 'Bloodsport' opens in a frenetic fashion, instantly injecting you with energy. The raw, catchy bass lines and a vocal delivery that shifts somewhere between Sleaford Mods and La Dispute set the tone. After a couple of minutes, the saxophone enters, adding a mystical dimension. This is not a decorative instrument for Maruja. It is embedded in their DNA and plays a crucial role in shaping their identity. They are masters at building tension, and when the explosions finally arrive, you will want to stand up, move your body, scream, and jump into the mosh pit. One could easily imagine that Maruja grew up listening to Rage Against the Machine, not only because of certain musical and vocal hints, but also because of their rebellious and socially conscious spirit. This becomes evident in the majestic 'Look Down On Us', a sublime composition that begins with tremendous energy and gradually morphs into different sonic entities. At times it dissolves, at times it resurfaces, offering subtle instrumental passages close to post rock that invite you to breathe and reflect on your life, the universe, and the context in which we exist. At their core, Maruja possess a deeply emotional and thoughtful spirit, which they channel through both lyrics and sound. Prepare yourself for the most moving moments, especially around the sixth minute of this track. The song that led me to this album was 'Saoirse,' and I hold it very close to my soul. It begins delicately, almost like a small jazz jam, with the saxophone taking the lead while bass and drums gradually build a subtle, nostalgic atmosphere. The addition of violins adds beautiful color, and a soft yet profound voice delivers phrases we will want to repeat and shout, such as "it's our differences that make us beautiful." That line carries not only musical beauty but cultural significance as well. We are a world of distinct yet complementary individuals, and perhaps we should see it through that lens of light rather than through the tyranny that too often prevails. 'Born to Die' is a ten-minute whirlwind of emotion that from its very first second establishes the protest driven soul of Maruja. The song unfolds slowly yet hypnotically, with tension built through guitars and restrained saxophone lines, while the voice declaims from deep within about the irony that we are all born only to die. Although the tempo remains steady, emotional intensity steadily rises. New textures appear constantly, and there is a clear progressive rock influence in the structure. With each cycle, the cry of "Born to Die" grows stronger. The drums introduce increasingly complex figures, the saxophone continues to paint the atmosphere, and the strings inject endless shades of emotion, together forming a controlled chaos. Just before the sixth minute, there is a pause, and the initial structure returns, only to give way moments later to a more driving rock section filled with energy and frenzy. It feels like the kind of catharsis we need if we truly wish to change the world. With 'Break the Tension', a sense of collective strength and protest emerges. The vocals blend punk urgency with hip hop cadence, supported by gritty bass lines, dynamic drumming, and a saxophone that can either build or release tension at will. We then move into another shorter piece, 'Trenches', which carries shades of Rage Against the Machine and perhaps even Run The Jewels. It is easy to chant along with the hip hop rhythm and nod your head with force, while the lyrics and instrumentation deliver yet another profound and powerful message. 'Zaytoun' is a four-minute introspective track where the musicians create layered textures and subtle noises that form countless atmospheres. Those distant screams generate a sense of chaos, but also of hope. Everything is in constant motion. It feels like a reflective interlude that prepares us for a powerful finale. That finale arrives with 'Reconcile', a ten-minute closing statement in which Maruja encapsulate their sound in a cohesive and compelling way. It begins with subtle passages that move between post rock and jazz, gradually transforming into their other sonic faces, with rock, hip hop, and punk always present. The transitions feel completely natural and never forced. The balance among instruments and the band's compositional and performance skills are remarkable. It is a brilliant ending to an album that came to make noise, and one that deserves to be celebrated and shared. I truly hope I can see Maruja live someday. Until then, I will be eagerly awaiting their next releases.

items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comWhat a beautiful release. Dewa Budjana is one of the flagship artists of MoonJune Records, a musician I discovered during the previous decade and who has kept me fascinated ever since, thanks to the sublime way he approaches the guitar. His playing carries an exquisite cadence deeply connected to spirituality, creating a combination where, in the end, the true beneficiary is not the body, but the soul itself. For this EP, inspired by his family, Budjana decided to revisit five compositions and record them alongside an orchestra. The chosen collaborators were the Czech Symphony Orchestra, with whom he achieved a marvelous convergence that allowed everything to flow naturally and efficiently, as if the magic had already been present in the atmosphere before the recording even began. While I have often mentioned that some albums can feel overly long, here the opposite happens: this EP leaves us wanting more, simply because it is that good. Everything begins with the delicious "Pranayama", whose seven minutes unfold with extraordinary elegance. The piece feels highly visual, as the different instrumental textures and melodic figures easily transport the listener to various imagined worlds. Naturally, it is Budjana's expressive guitar that guides the experience, but the orchestra and the subtle percussive elements enrich the atmosphere with emotion and multicultural depth. Interestingly, each following track becomes slightly shorter. "On The Way Home" carries a spiritual and somewhat folk oriented atmosphere, with the acoustic guitar opening the path into new territories, while the wind instruments become especially important this time around. The rhythm remains semi slow, offering a warm embrace for the soul in a moment of contemplation and calm. Budjana's acoustic guitar work is remarkably clean and elegant, yet never loses its emotional power. With "Sasih Sadha", the music moves closer to classical territory. Of course, the presence of an orchestra naturally evokes that feeling, but compositionally speaking, the piece genuinely leans toward a classical sensibility. What makes it particularly interesting are the subtle electronic elements introduced throughout, along with the shifts in mood and intensity mainly driven by the wind section. A beautifully harmonious composition. "Dreamland" is one of my favorite moments on the EP. The bass work is exquisite, subtle yet memorable. The track flows wonderfully, like wandering through open fields while appreciating nature alongside the people who bring meaning and warmth into our lives. Its calm rhythm embraces the listener, guiding us gently, while every small detail, every instrument, and every passage leads toward the same destination: pure satisfaction. The EP concludes with "Karma", the calmest composition of all and a finale that truly feels like a farewell. It gives the impression of having reached a long sought destination, as if, after so much effort, magic finally carried us exactly where we dreamed of being. Good karma arrives here to embrace the soul, and Dewa Budjana together with the orchestra knew perfectly well how to achieve it.

items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comWhat a marvelous album! I feel truly fortunate to discover music created by incredibly talented people from all around the world, and Spanish composer and drummer Xavi Reija is undoubtedly one of them. With a long and respected career, and now a familiar name within the roster of MoonJune Records, Reija has showcased his abilities across a vast number of albums, whether as the main creative force behind a project or as a guest musician contributing his distinctive touch. Now, in 2026, accompanied by his Electric Quintet, Reija delivers "Nu Breed", a majestic work that, without hesitation, has become my favorite release within his catalog. The album features an ensemble of top caliber musicians, beginning with Dusan Jevtovic, another artist I came to know thanks to the MoonJune family, a remarkably skilled guitarist who has built a wonderful musical chemistry with Reija. Of course, the success of this record also relies heavily on the extraordinary talents of Bernat Hern�ndez on bass, Tom�s Fosch on keyboards, and Rafael Garc�s on saxophone. Reija has established himself as a true master of experimental drumming, incorporating elements from different genres and techniques into his playing. While I may not have connected equally with some of his previous works, I must say that from the very first listen of "Nu Breed", I was completely captivated. This is an exquisite release where jazz, progressive rock, and avant-garde converge in a forty minute journey divided into eight compositions that genuinely stands among my favorite releases of 2026. Everything begins with "Dreamscape Room", a track that delights us with such a free and organic approach to creating and sharing music. The quintet feels completely connected, as if their chemistry extends far beyond the recording studio and into real life itself, because there is a beautiful energy and natural flow that fills both our ears and souls with high quality music. I particularly enjoyed Garc�s' work on the saxophone here. Rock enters the equation with "Are You Religious?", where the band clearly shifts toward a heavier, more intense, and electric sound. This can be heard in Jevtovic's guitar work, but also in the attitude and interplay of the entire ensemble. Naturally, Reija's drumming undergoes its own transformation as well, offering a masterclass in blending rock, prog, and jazz through an experimental lens that feels both unique and unmistakably tied to Reija and the MoonJune universe. This is one of my favorite compositions on the album, a track I deeply enjoy and one that continues to reveal new details and emotions with every listen. The title "Dusan Song" may serve as a clue to what lies ahead, or perhaps simply as a tribute to the quintet's guitarist. Yet the piece is far from a monologue. Instead, it is a construction built equally by all five musicians, perfectly reflecting the jazz fusion spirit they embody, along with that inherent avant-garde and experimental edge flowing through their veins. Naturally, Jevtovic shines throughout several passages, which is exactly what one would expect from such a talented musician. And indeed, from the very first bass notes Hern�ndez plays to introduce "Dream Land", I felt immediately drawn into the piece. As the seconds passed and the rest of the instruments entered, that attraction only grew stronger. Jazz fusion is present through elegant and fluid sounds that constantly evolve and challenge themselves, guiding the listener into a wonderful multisensory experience. The dialogue between bass and drums is particularly powerful, and although those were the first instruments to capture my attention, every musician fulfills an essential role. That is why the saxophone emerges as a guide in certain moments, while the guitar hypnotizes us in others. "We Keep Walking" opens with the progressive side of the band through Fosch's keyboards and the layers he gradually builds, soon joined by drums, bass, guitar, and saxophone to launch another captivating journey. That progressive fusion essence remains throughout the composition, filled with emotional highs and lows and an endless display of figures and phrases from each musician, resulting in a piece that feels electrifying in some moments and subtle in others. Another personal favorite. With "Reflections", the palette of sounds and colors changes drastically. Here, the tempo slows down and the music enters a more experimental territory where each instrument expresses itself with total freedom and without barriers. I could describe this track as a sort of interlude within the album. The title track, "Nu Breed", is absolutely delicious, a frenetic journey through progressive fusion featuring sublime changes in rhythm and mood that can leave the listener in a state of exhilaration. I love the different rhythmic figures Reija plays and the way he adapts his drumming whenever another instrument takes the spotlight, allowing each musician to shine naturally and comfortably. In particular, I adore the passages where he works side by side with Garc�s, whose explosive saxophone is beautifully supported by the atmospheric keyboard layers created by Fosch. Shifting rhythms, hypnotic atmospheres, playful moments, and raw power all coexist here. At times, the spirit of Weather Report inevitably comes to mind, both individually and collectively. A magnificent composition. Finally, the quintet closes the album with "Two Sides". I had been thinking it throughout the record, but this track confirmed it for me: the spirit of Frank Zappa is also present here. The piece perfectly reflects the creativity displayed across the entire album, carrying that progressive fusion essence infused with experimentation and avant-garde sensibilities. Once again, I also sense the influence of Weather Report, which appears repeatedly throughout the record. A wonderful closing track for a truly fabulous album. Congratulations to Xavi Reija and company, because they have just released a genuine musical gem.

items.body: Review by alainPP — This is the second album in a trilogy marking the band's return after a long hiatus'their eighth overall'exploring the group's inner journey through a gothic-prog lens."Sanguis" opens with Endre's nostalgic vintage organ, Kjetil's baritone vocals, and a fluid heavy riff that is neither pompous nor solemn. It evolves into a groovy, hypnotic, and majestic soundscape, joined by screamed vocals. The lyrics'dealing with domestic violence and its bloody aftermath'steer the music between light and dark, bridging the gap between atmospheric prog metal and the somber doom of The Gathering. "Loneliness Untold, Loneliness Unfold" features a cinematic intro in the style of an archaic ballad. Organ, acoustic guitar, and raw, anguished vocals define this moment of solitude'cherished by some, feared by many others."Sweet to the Point of Bitter" bursts in, shattering the mood with a barrage from Jonathan's double-kick drum kit and a deluge of tearful, melancholic guitars. Stein's soaring vocals contrast the brutality of the cutting riff against the languid foundation of the infectious chorus."I Am Time" extends the visceral atmosphere, reflecting the doubts inherent in a tragic tale; this is highlighted by orchestration that bridges the 1970s and the new millennium. Bj'rn delivers soothing, majestic, and atmospheric solos; the melody oozes emotion, with a majestic trumpet providing a breath of air'a way to avoid counting the time as it accelerates with advancing age."Fire in Ice" begins with an ambient intro before launching into a frenetic heavy riff driven by thick keyboard tones and double-kick drumming. With its measured vocals, the track plays out as a martial electro-rock ballad, gorging on heavy atmosphere set against soft singing'a classic oxymoron. The song's drift feels oppressive, fanning the embers of this icy air as it snakes into our memory to curl up and stay. The finale machine-guns the air and the ears'a throwback to the sound of yesteryear'before the cinematic feel returns. "Lunar Tale" is as dark as the moon, featuring classical piano and austere vocals'a contemplative ballad about battered memories. Synths amplify the nostalgic aura, leaving one curious about the upcoming album. Ingrid's flute brings serenity, while the outro'evoking an unsettling twilight'sets a signature dreamlike mood: an orgasmic melancholy. "Sanguis (Blood Ties)" is included as a bonus track, ready for a potential radio edit'a nod to the days when such things mattered. And the urge to listen again speaks to the track's spellbinding melody.Green Carnation continues to evolve, offering a more mature, rich sound driven by prominent keyboards. The tracks are dark and somber, with echoes of Emperor and gothic death metal shifting into powerful post-metal and prog-heavy rock'a languid melancholy charged with melodic tension.(4.25)

The album was released through theArt-beat Label in January 2016. It�s the successor to "2nd Hands" from December 2006. Formed in 2001and having only released three full-length studio albums in the years 2001-2026 it�s safe to saythat The Gourishankar/Gourishanker aren�t the most prolific artist in terms of output quantity.Since the release of "2nd Hands" there�s been an almost complete change of personal, as onlyAlexandr "Nomy" Agranson remains from the lineup who recorded the two preceding albums. Agransonperforms all guitars, bass, keyboards, and programming as well as co-producing "The World Unreal".New in the lineup are Jason Offen (vocals, co-production), and Svetoslav Bogdanov (drums,percussion).The most obvious Rush and Dream Theater influences which were pretty dominant on the first twoalbums are not as strong an influence on "The World Unreal", which generally sounds a bit differentcompared to the preceding albums. Offen has a more regular voice than Vlad MJ Whiner whom he hasreplaced and now I�m no longer thinking of a James LaBrie/Geddy Lee clone, but instead I�m thinkingof a warm and melancholic delivery closer to Mariusz Duda from Riverside/Lunatic Soul. In thatrespect "The World Unreal" is a more accessible release, but Gourishankar still occasionallyproduces some pretty technical and challenging progressive rock, which requires your full attention.It�s just a lot more subdued, atmospheric, and accessible this time around. It�s unfortunately also less energetic and as "The World Unreal" features a sound production whichlacks in the power department and at times sounds a bit too much like it was recorded on a computerin someone�s bedroom, I�m not completely satisfied with the new musical direction of Gourishankar.Upon conclusion "The World Unreal" ends up being a "beware of what you wish for" type release forme, as I was asking for a more song oriented compositional approach in my reviews of the band�spreceding album releases, but when I listen to "The World Unreal" I miss the greatly energetic andever changing nature of the earlier releases (I guess the poor band just can�t seem to satisfy me).A 2.5 - 3 star (55%) rating is warranted.

items.body: Review by SilverLight59 — I have been wanting to review this album for a while now, so here we are. Released in 2024, Stranger Skies is the fourth studio album from Ellesmere. It clocks in at a modest 47 minutes and is broken into six tracks. The first four cover about half of the overall time and revolve around a cold arctic world, while the final two tracks are longer and fill out the second half of the album. These two change the narrative direction to a warmer setting and a different sonic landscape. While not necessarily an outright concept album, it does seem to have something of a cohesive concept that links it all together, and the stunning album artwork further suggests this.This is a heavy, well at least semi heavy, progressive project masterminded by Italian musician Roberto Vitelli with the help of a number of talented guests. The album blends classic 1970s symphonic prog sensibilities with modern production. Unlike previous albums such as 2020's 'Wyrd" that was largely instrumental, this one goes all in on having a vocalist, John Wilkinson, as well as backing vocalists which has created a tectonic shift in their sound. While past Ellesmere efforts leaned into sprawling, dazzling instrumental passages, Stranger Skies pivots to a more vocal oriented songwriting approach. This choice grounds the compositions, making the overall experience far more accessible, direct, and memorable. So, let's take a look at the tracks"Northwards": This starts with a beautiful heavy symphonic flourish for a couple minutes that has an almost "Edward Scissor Hands" deja vu vibe about it. Credit to Clive Nolan (pendragon, Arena) for his wonderful keyboards here. Going along with the album art, I imagine a blue crystalline ice cave to go with this opening sequence. From here it springs forward with a synth lead running point, and full band quickly joins into a much heavier follow up. This intensity goes clear to the end without let up. Lyrics immediately follow the full band introduction with John Wilkinson's urgent vocals taking center stage. Musically and vocally, there is a strong reference to early Genesis as Wilkinson sounds eerily similar to Phil Collins, and the song structure and style, although more intense, picks up flavor of classic early Genesis. Perhaps the most accessible track and a great start! (9.5/10)"Tundra": This one opens big and bold driven by catchy guitar melodies from Giacomo Anselmi and syncopated synth rhythms. Wilkinson's vocal performance again strongly draws comparison with Phil Collins' era of Genesis, particularly during the A Trick of the Tail period. The drumming is powerful driving the song along with real energy. An extra feature here is the lush backing vocals by Riccardo Romano, building toward an unexpected, intricate Yes-style a cappella harmony segment reminiscent of "Leave It". The track concludes with a nice guitar solo that builds up and suddenly plays out. Another great track! (9/10)"Crystallized": This changes pace entirely and starts with a lovely classical acoustic guitar piece by Graeme Taylor (Gryphon). Approaching two minutes In, electric guitar, synths, drums, ramp up, and saxophone by guest David Jackson (Van Der Graaf Generator) breaks in. His contribution is angular, complex, chaotic, and fiery evoking the avant garde tension of some of Van Der Graaf Generators' iconic work. This is the lone instrumental track on this offering, and a pretty good one at that. (8/10)"Arctica": This is the shortest track, compact, high-energy, featuring dense layers of backing vocals. The propulsive, rhythmic interplay between Vitelli's driving basslines and Mattias Olsson's (�nglag�rd) precision drumming carries heavy Rush overtones, closely mirroring the tight, punchy energy of "Tom Sawyer". The final third of the track the synths come to the fore and help lead the charge to the end of the song, and the end of the 'cold' portion of the album. (8/10)"Stranger Skies": The 12-minute title track seamlessly starts and anchors the album's 'warmer' second half. It begins with a gentle near acapella vocal that melts into a church organ like synth (shades of early Wakeman) and John Hackett's delicate flute work, which lingers in and out through the whole track. As it builds, the piece balances intricate time signatures with an anthemic recurring melody, featuring vintage Mellotron waves from Stefano Vicarelli and additional keyboards by Bob Hodges. About half way, the track pauses to catch its breath and then the church organ sound comes back, but with once again, a more angular edge to the track. A very nice electric guitar lead with flute accompaniment builds up and winds this one down to its final quiet moments that fade away with an acoustic finish. Very nice! (9/10)"Another World": With the final 11-minute epic, Ellesmere chooses to close out the record with a dynamic, rhythm-driven symphonic prog tour de force. It acts as a warm, concluding link, deliberately bookending the icy, frigid themes of the album's first half. It features another standout performance from David Jackson providing fiery saxophone licks that help drive the melodies of the electric guitar work, and a grand keyboard finale from former Flower Kings maestro Tomas Bodin. Additionally, Vitelli weaves dense shifting keyboard textures that are complimented by drummer Olsson's powerful prog rock chops. This a big piece of music! The track serves as a satisfying conclusion to the overarching narrative of travel and discovering unexplored realms. By unexpectedly reprising the chorus from the opening track, "Northwards", it ties the entire journey together. All that remains is a psychedelic, gentle piano and atmospheric outro with children's voices overlayed, again with a hint of 'scissor hands' essence but more obscure this time, that feels like stepping through a portal bringing the traveler home. (9/10)For those not familiar with Ellesmere, Stranger Skies is the album to make introduction with. It comes across as polished and technically flawless. The incorporation of the guest talent by Vitelli has elevated it considerably over previous efforts. The pivot toward robust, memorable vocal melodies makes it more accessible and memorable. Still, true to the past there is substantial muscle and exercising of instrumental prowess. A strong effort indeed! If you like the referenced guests, bands , or music, this should be right up your alley. Good news as the band has officially announced they are working on new studio material. They tend to run an average of three years between releases, so we are hopefully getting close. But for now, 4 stars for the Stranger Skies.

items.body: Let me say straight away that this is a very good performance of Carmina Burana. The choral singing is excellent, the singers balanced well forward so we hear them at every dynamic level. The soloists sing well, each having clearly thought about the text and its characterization. The orchestra plays with energy and exactitude. The wide, deep soundstage lets us hear its tummy-rumbling power at climaxes, but there are quieter moments where the ensemble and solo playing is finely turned. The different components come together in the second part (In Taberna) and through much of the third (Cour d’amours). Conductor Jader Bignamini has a sharp vision of how this music should sound, and has convinced his performers to realize it. Carmina Burana Amazon Presto Apple But his interpretation too often strays from what Orff intends. Some tempos are slower than they should be, but more troubling is Bignamini’s unwillingness to generate enough forward momentum. Readers might argue that this is an issue of personal preference, and it is true that all this listener’s favorite performances of Carmina take under an hour (Bignamini takes just under 61 minutes). But there is a reference recording, endorsed by the composer, which should perhaps serve as a guide for how this music is meant to be performed. Orff was present for Eugen Jochum’s 1967 DG recording with the Chorus and Orchestra of the Deutsche Oper Berlin and three stellar soloists. It has remained in the catalogue ever since, rightly hailed as a classic. That is, at least in part, because Orff was thrilled by the drive and rhythmic verve of Jochum’s interpretation, which takes less than 56 minutes. Jochum highlights the music’s primitivism, the purposeful stripping away of sophistication in favor of raw, elemental force. Orff’s incessant ostinatos and percussive orchestration create earthy, visceral energy, and Jochum understands that, even if the 1960s sound cannot capture it all as well as a digital recording. Bignamini, on the other hand, often seeks to add sophistication back into the score, to make it more profound than Orff intends. Compare his opening chorus with performances by Ozawa and Rattle (Philips/Universal and Warner Classics). Neither conductor is significantly faster than Bignamini, but both push forward in a way that creates a frenetic atmosphere that makes the Detroit performance seem cautious. Bignamini’s second movement is not significantly slower than Ozawa, Rattle, Blomstedt (Decca) or Muti (Warner Classics), but his more legato phrasing and articulation weigh the music down. And in the sixth-movement orchestral dance, he suddenly slows for the flute and timpani duet — why? The flute playing is beautiful, but are beauty and shapeliness what the composer wanted? Again, it strikes me as adding sophistication to music that is expressly meant to reject that quality. The Detroit Symphony Orchestra. Photo © Sarah Smarch. The use of a countertenor (Reginald Mobley) instead of a tenor also goes against the score. The tessitura of “Olim lacus colueram” is infamously high for a reason — the swan is lamenting that it is being roasted to death over a fire. Most tenors sound uncomfortable singing it, which is exactly what Orff wanted. Mobley, by contrast, sounds too beautiful. Baritone Andrzej Filończyk offers vivid characterization, painted in bold colors, but Fischer-Dieskau (Jochum), Hampson (Ozawa) and Gerhaher (Rattle), all of them excellent Lieder singers, find greater textual expression. And in the final movements (tracks 21–23), soprano Chen Reiss lacks the vocal mastery that makes Gundula Janowitz (Jochum) and, most especially, Arleen Auger (Muti) so ravishing. The strongest part of the performance is the choral and orchestral work, though I cannot say it betters what we hear from San Francisco (Blomstedt), London (Muti), or Berlin (Ozawa and Rattle). Pentatone’s engineering is truthful and makes no effort to turn the production into a ‘sonic blockbuster.’ First-rate liner notes often point the reader toward the text, yet this booklet offers neither text nor translation. In an already crowded field, this very good performance does not challenge existing recommendations. items.body: Tiffadelic “There She Go” is the new single from Tiffadelic, a darkwave and dark synthwave artist from Detroit, released on 10 July 2026. “There She Go” follows her early-2026 single “Blood Bath” and her 2025 debut album “Retrosynthesis Vol. I”, and is available on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. Tiffadelic brings a dark synthwave that pairs brooding vocals with minimal, beat-driven synth. Battle Chamber Music describes the track as “a dark synthwave fantasy about the intoxicating pull between desire and uncertainty.” Inside Tiffadelic’s ‘There She Go’ Tiffadelic wrote the music and lyrics for “There She Go”. She recorded the vocals at Battle Chamber Studio in Detroit, where Steve Greene handled vocal engineering, mixing and mastering. Tai Design Co. and Dark Visionaries created the cover art. The single is available on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. “There She Go” continues a run of 2026 releases. It follows “Blood Bath”, whose video premiered on 26 June 2026, and extends the production partnership with Greene that shaped both that single and Tiffadelic’s debut album. About Tiffadelic Tiffadelic is a Detroit-based artist who mixes darkwave, post-punk, minimal wave and synth, and describes herself as a “Black Goth” artist. She released her debut album, “Retrosynthesis Vol. I”, in September 2025 through Darthpira Records, a nine-track record issued on limited-edition gold cassette and produced with Steve Greene at Battle Chamber Studio. Earlier singles include “I Tried” and “Nazareth (B.O.P)”. The “Blood Bath” single arrived in early 2026, with its video premiere on 26 June 2026. “There She Go”, released on 10 July 2026, is her next single, again recorded and mixed with Greene at Battle Chamber Studio. Verified background on the artist beyond her releases is limited at the time of writing.

items.body: Manchester band Sea Fever, whose line-up draws on New Order and Section 25, released the compilation LP “Special Australian Edition” through the Brisbane label Trans:Com on 31 October 2025. The record is a limited edition of 500 copies on blue regrind vinyl and gathers singles from the group’s first two albums alongside new remixes by Australian producers. Special Australian Edition by Sea Fever What is on Sea Fever’s ‘Special Australian Edition’ The album pairs six singles from Sea Fever’s studio LPs with newly commissioned remixes. “Go To Ground”, “Loose Cut” and “Breaking Out” come from the 2025 album “Surface Sound”, while “Beleaguered Land”, “De Facto” and “Crossed Wires” come from the 2021 debut “Folding Lines”. Australian producers Boxcar, Alieonix, Vision Four 5, hedfog and Dharma Buffer supply the remixes, including two Boxcar versions of “Loose Cut” and a pair of hedfog reworks of “Breaking Out”. Trans:Com founder Dennis Remmer handled the release concept and art direction, with band photography by Anthony Harrison and original artwork by Andy Kiff. The LP is sold through the label’s Bandcamp page and in independent record stores across Australia and New Zealand. About Sea Fever Sea Fever is a five-piece formed in Manchester. The band mixes atmospheric synths, indie guitars and driving rhythms, and is fronted by Iwan Gronow, who has played with Haven and in Johnny Marr‘s band, and Beth Cassidy of Section 25. The line-up is completed by Tom Chapman and Phil Cunningham, both of New Order, and Elliot Barlow of Folks. The group issued its debut album “Folding Lines” in 2021 through Kartel and followed it with “Surface Sound” in 2025 on Cosmic Glue. Songs on both records were written by the band, with lyrics by Gronow and Cassidy and production led by Tom Chapman. The “Special Australian Edition” draws that catalogue together for a territory-specific pressing, adding remixes from the Australian electronic scene around Trans:Com.

items.body: Tranxhaine “Anamnèse” is the debut album from Tranxhaine, a French darkwave, gothic rock and post-punk project, self-released on July 10, 2026. “Anamnèse” gathers eight tracks and is issued as a digital album on Bandcamp, with a T-shirt edition made by Xavier Pinel. Anamnèse by TRANXHAINE Tranxhaine mixes gothic rock and post-punk with electronic textures, and sums up its intent in one line: “Traumas, but make them danceable.” The title is the French word for anamnesis, a recollection of the past, and the project describes the record as an autobiographical set: “This album carries years of memories, questions, fears and fragments of a life that slowly found its way into music. Every track is a chapter, every sound a piece of a story that shaped who I am.” “Anamnèse” runs eight tracks: “TRAMADOLL”, “Post Suicide Club”, “Small and Paranoid”, “Benzodya Zeppelin”, “Ni Catharsis Ni Pardon”, “Foggy Body Mindless Brain”, “ULTRAVIOLENCE” and “ULTRAVIOLENCE II (The Autopsy of Me)”. Three of them reached Bandcamp first as 2026 singles: “Ni Catharsis Ni Pardon” in March, “Post Suicide Club” in April and “Foggy Body Mindless Brain” in May. About Tranxhaine Tranxhaine is a darkwave, gothic rock and post-punk project based in France. It does not list a lineup on its official pages, and the album text is written in the first person. The project self-describes as “Traumas, but make them danceable.” Tranxhaine’s releases all date from 2026. The project opened with the single “Ni Catharsis Ni Pardon” in March 2026, followed by “Post Suicide Club” in April and “Foggy Body Mindless Brain” in May. All three appear on the debut album. “Anamnèse” followed on July 10, 2026 as an eight-track digital release with a T-shirt edition. The album is the project’s first full-length after that opening run of singles.

items.body: Hey folks. The Senior Staff were on the decks here in Vancouver last weekend at the fabulous Red Room here in Vancouver, and as always it served as a reminder that while we track plenty of new music, there’s no telling what might hit with the audience that comes out to a goth-industrial format nightclub in 2026. There were certainly some surprising reactions to cuts new and old, and those kinds of revelations are part of what makes the game of DJing so fun for us with over 50 years combined experience in the field. All the more reason to keep digging up new songs, which is where Tracks comes in this week. Years Of Denial Years of Denial, “We Operate on Each Other” We’re admirers of French/Czech duo Years of Denial for a lot of reasons, but primarily for the fluidity with which they switch up their style and still retain their identity. In the case of new cut “We Operate on Each Other” we have a pretty sweet upbeat, minimal synth touched electro flavour that feels both modern and classic. And like all their material, there’s a real clean, uncluttered production sensibility that keeps it bumping in headphones or on a big system. We Operate on Each Other by Years of Denial Soft Vein, “Learning To Talk” Speaking of clean and upbeat synths, the latest single from one-man California project Soft Vein leading to Justin Chamberlain’s third LP under the name continues the move towards a much brighter and melodic sound. Sure, there’s still plenty of “mood” in the mix, but like “All We’ve Known Of Heaven” before it this points to a real understanding of the songwriting sitting beneath any number of rich, classic synthpop tunes (optimistic or no), and a song about the joy and ease that comes as a relationship deepens is a legitimately sweet thing to encounter. Learning to Talk by Soft Vein Stabbing Westward, “Crushing Me” We’ve said it many times, and we’ll keep saying it: Stabbing Westward are underrated, and for dumb reasons. The main culprit is probably the crossover success of their major label debut Wither, Blister, Burn and Peel, which both got them tons of radio play, but also earned them the contempt of industrial snobs too cool to enjoy their super catchy, well produced industrial rock cuts. Since reactivating the band has been doing some of the best work of their career, and is bringing some of their current approach to their big record with Wither – ReWired, a fully rerecorded version of the album. How is it gonna sound? Have a listen to deep album cut Crushing Me, it should set you up right. Wither – ReWired by Stabbing Westward Blood Rave, “The Burning Field” The Wie Ein Gott label serves as a base of operations for Johannes Stabel’s celebrated XTR Human project, but it’s also brought us enjoyable releases from the likes of Nero, Termination_800, and Baroque. The label’s new comp offers existing and unreleased work from Feudal, Static Ghost, Dildox, and the like, including this very tasty new slice from Blood Rave, which brings vintage Front Line together with more melodic contemporary dancefloor electro. Made By Humans by Blood Rave Ash Code, “Dancing to the Noise (Tobias Bernstrup remix)” While Italian darkwavers Ash Code are generally pretty solid when it comes to putting out dancefloor friendly club cuts, this remix of their track by the always reliable Tobias Bernstrup brings a real different flavour. There’s a lot of Italo in that octave bass, and the stutter and delay on the vocals and orch hits really give it that old 12″ dub vibe. Dancing To The Noise (Tobias Bernstrup REMIX) by Ash Code I.M.P., “Rules Of Engagement” The latest discovery of X-IMG records doesn’t exactly sidestep the TBM remit that the label of Sarin’s Emad Dabiri has had as its focus from the beginning, but certainly draws a line between current iterations of that style and a much more low-fi and scrappy vision of EBM associated with second generation German acts like Armageddon Dildos. Very little to go on with regards to I.M.P. as a project other than being Seattle based, but rangy and pissed-off fare like this is very easy to listen to. Rules of Engagement by I.M.P. items.body: Bands: Deathspiral of Inherited Suffering, Elysian Blaze, Panegyrist, Maerund | Album: Sunthema | Genre: Black metal, Progressive metal, Post-metal | Year: 2026 From: Memphis, USA; Adelaide, Australia; Chicago, USA; Chicago, USA (I think) | Label: Rubeus Obex (USA); I, Voidhanger (Europe) For fans of: Cormorant, Enslaved, Batushka Bandcamp I first found out about this record through Rate Your Music’s handy “Upcoming Releases” feature. It was there that I saw Panegyrist had their first new music since 2018 coming out! Their lone LP, Hierurgy, is a stunning, unique release. It blends avant-garde black metal with liturgical music and lyrics so dense and obscure that I feel like I need a theology degree to understand them. Sunthema, the four-way split LP with Panegyrist and three other acts, continues on that trend. (Side note: Personally, I would have transliterated the Greek “συνθεμα” as “synthema,” but to each their own. The word is more often found in its plural form, synthemata, and it refers to any signs, symbols, or material tokens, especially those associated with certain rituals. Esoteric terms and ideas are prominent on this record.) All four acts here weave their brands of forward-thinking metal with Christian mysticism to make something powerful and enthralling.  This album begins with three songs from Deathspiral of Inherited Suffering, a Memphis-based trio whose only other output was on a different split LP from I, Voidhanger back in 2018. “Grailcrushing Wounds” features buzzy, scouring blackened death metal at a deliberate pace. The sense of weight is enormous, with the plodding rhythm and jittery lead guitar in constant tension with one another. The outro of this song also features some wonderfully eerie electric piano for some much-appreciated variation. “Resurrectionist” explodes right out of the gate, with a fiery, apocalyptic tone. The gut-rattling riffs on this song bounce around, constantly shifting and morphing; some provide a deep-down rumble, and others provide sharp, biting contrast. Concluding DoIS’s contribution to Sunthema is “Houses of Abysmal Masks”. They lean into death metal most obviously here, with a pervasive dark and occult mood. Elysian Blaze–an Australian atmospheric black metal act–offers up one 17-minute opus for Sunthema. “Ascenturion” is starkly different from what preceded it. The vocals are gentle and airy, and the overall sound is hazy and obscure. There’s a sense of both desperation and triumph as this piece progresses. The band skillfully juxtaposes tinkling keys and clean vocals against crushing, doom-influenced guitars. There’s a nearly meditative feel to the main riff of this song.This band demonstrates great textural and atmospheric variation, drawing heavily from post-metal and post-rock. The soundscape the band builds is crushing and majestic all at once, and this composition feels shorter than it really is. Panegyrist’s pair of songs are next. Both clock in at 12 minutes and 14 seconds (I’m sure there’s some esoteric numerological reason for that), and the first is “Twilight Take Our Faces”. Unorthodox riffs rush forth, as tangled guitar lines traverse uncommon scales. This work takes on the maximalist sound of Panegyrist’s debut, but it shows amazing maturation and development. Dissonant black metal merges with moments of melodic power metal and liturgical chanting to make something truly impressive and inspiring.  “Luciferous”  opens with cascading guitars and tumbling drums. The guitars twist and slash, making for a fantastically disorienting experience. Growls and angelic choirs weave into one another as this epic barrels furiously forward. Hints of classic prog rock crop up on occasion, especially when piano enters to slow things down for a moment. Heading into this epic’s final movement, the music takes on some triumphal tones. The brutality and strife inherent to black metal is still there, but the composition somehow is still uplifting. On the rare occasions Christian music has come up on this site, I’ve consistently lambasted it for being hokey and unimaginative. Panegyrist, though, shows how to invoke a sense of mystical glory and wonder. Their music feels like a divine revelation. Most Christian music I’ve heard is the musical equivalent of a nondenominational church in a strip mall. This example, however, is an auditory basilica. If Panegyrist had put this music out on their own, it would be hard to knock it off the top of my year-end list. The fourth and final act present on Sunthema is a new band, Maerund. It’s a one-man project from one of the co-owners of Rubeus Obex, the label distributing this album in the US. After doing a little digging, I think they’re based out of Chicago, since the other co-owner of the label is Elijah Tamu of Panegyrist. “HAVAH LAYAHLAH” reminds me of Batushka. It’s stormy, noisy, doomy black metal with chanted vocals. The clean vocals have a mildly processed sound to them, which I love as well. This song mostly ruminates on one riff, but it works, and things remain exciting for the whole runtime. “Transcendence of the World Through the Cross Inverted” stays in a similar vein, but there are some creative inclusions with unusual percussion. Ultimately, though, these two songs are pretty similar and don’t both feel necessary. “Manna Pharmaika” has a riff that’s a bit more distinctive than the two preceding songs, and the chanted vocals fit the hypnotic nature of the backing. Maerund shows some more variety on this track than on the previous two songs, and that’s much appreciated. The music is furious and pounding, but with some nice internal variation. Closing out the album is “Red Crystal Lattice”. It’s another intense composition, and I really like the way the bass is strummed to provide the melodic lead. Sunthema is a dense, challenging record, but it’s a resounding success. Each of the bands here shows a unique take on progressive and avant-garde black metal that makes the four quarters stand out. At the same time, they all complement one another. The dense, esoteric lyrics and complex musical arrangements show what black metal can do when pushed to its artistic extremes. Score: 91/100

items.body: Editor's note: just like 2025 and 2024 before it, we are eschewing a "classic", big ol' list of albums we liked from 2026 so far. Lists are fun but they make no sense ("this album is number 12 and this album is number 9" are words uttered by the insane). Instead, we will be using the next few weeks to highlight our favorite trends, releases, shows, cover art, experiences, and more from the first half of this (musically) excellent year. It should be common knowledge by now (for the blog’s readership at least) that I have left narratives in the rear view mirror. As I’ve said before, I think that’s just the virtue of the passage of time: you can only see your carefully constructed structures fade away so many times before you give up building them in the first place. But that doesn’t mean we’re not allowed to add any structure to our analysis of music; far from it. Instead, all we have to do is try to focus on smaller scopes. When we try to understand years as arbitrary units of time, and the cycles of releases that come with things like finances, listener fatigue, marketing schedules, and the such, then we find that we understand more, not less, of why some things are happening.But there are phenomena that defy that sort of reading as well. They don’t sit quite well in either of the buckets. They’re not grand narratives on one side nor totally random occurrences on the other and that forces us to deploy and oft-memed perspective: nuance. Here’s an example for you: in 2026, there were many, many excellent releases in the field of technical/progressive thrash metal. We’ve spoken about on the blog before how even using the term causes people to scratch their heads because the sub-genre flowered briefly at the end of the 90’s and then faded away. To be sure, not all bands are gone; Voivod has been making music ever since then after all. But also to be sure, there hasn’t been a “wave” of technical thrash metal so much as droplets here or there, excellent albums but not really anything constituting a “revival”. Aletheia by Wildhunt But here we are in 2026 and let me just rattle off the list of bands: Wildhunt, Bekor Qilish, Cryptic Shift, Microwaves, Inscribed. I missed a few, I’m sure; those are just the ones I really liked (and that don’t use AI in their music, cough). That’s more than just an album here or there. It doesn’t quite make sense to pass this off as “release cycles”; most of these bands have not released an album in a few good years. It’s also not a micro-scene (local to a specific city) or even a scene located on a certain style of technical thrash. Cryptic Shift is ultra-technical and intricate while Wildhunt hits on the more sweeping, progressive, heavy metal vibes of the style. But they all congregate around fast riffs made complex by composition, instrument choice, or just sheer scope.On the other hand, I bet you that next year, and the year after that even, won’t have ten more technical thrash metal albums or at least not any as good as most of these. So if you jump the gun and start talking about a “renaissance” or a “revival”, you’re going to look pretty silly very soon (trust me, I’ve been there). So what are we to do? We can’t just shrug and say “oh this is all coincidence” and we also don’t want to say “the stars have ordained that technical thrash metal must return!” So let me offer you a nuanced middle ground - technical thrash metal has always been around as a style of metal. After all, we named Voivod above but there have been other bands working in the style all across these last three decades or so since it began.  Consecrated Abysses Of Dread by BEKOR QILISH Think of technical thrash metal as a potentiality or a color in a palette, if you’d prefer something less abstract. There was always the possibility of someone, anyone, reaching out for that color and making the potential real (woof). And so, whenever someone does that, it’s not really a surprise and it’s not random; it’s one of the ways in which metal can be made. But nor is there a grand narrative at play, some aligning of cursed stars which makes the genre suddenly popular. Rather, artists reach for a certain color and it’s not a surprise that some of them reach for the same one. Sometimes, the conditions of a current point in time can nudge the hand and make more of them want to paint a certain type of picture and, when that happens, they all reach into the same tool box.This also explains why all of the albums I'm going to link to in this post don't sound the same. It's not about a certain sound being adhered to but rather a sort of style influencing or inspiring a larger group of bands. Some of the bands are melodic; others rely on soul-crushing dissonance and intricacy. But they all have that edge to them, that combination of thrash's speed, progressive metal's flamboyant technicality, and bits of pieces from jazz, heavy metal, death metal, and more. There is something in the air, as if all of the bands are emanating from a common source upon which they bifurcate and fractal into different, yet similar, vectors.And there is the only positive statement I am willing to risk committing to: there is something in the air which calls forth the mode of technical thrash metal. I leave it to the reader to try and think about some answers for what that is as I am sure there is more than one. But I would like you to consider my favorite explanation: as things become more plastic, more sloppified, less human, more fake and polished but actually ugly (yes because of AI but more because of the social trends which gave birth to AI like, you know, fascism) the more we yearn for authenticity. We would like to replace the vapid joy of smoothness for the raw pleasure of friction. We want less marketing and more truth, less appeal and more passion, less consumption and more feasting. And what is more authentic, gritty, frictionful (that’s a word, shut up), and uncompromising than a genre known for taking something already very fast and making it also very complex? Overspace & Supertime by Cryptic Shift Temporal Shifter by Microwaves Upon the Twisted Throne by Inscribed
